question: X36
answer:
# NASA-STD-4003A — Class R (EMI/RF) Bond: What the Standard Actually Requires

## 1. Bottom line

**There is no maximum RF impedance, in ohms at a stated frequency, for a Class R bond in NASA-STD-4003A.** The standard does not state an impedance limit in ohms, and it does not state a frequency at which such a limit would apply. The premise of the question — that a single ohm value at a stated frequency exists and can be read out of the standard — is not correct.

What the standard *does* impose on a Class R joint is a **dc resistance limit of 2.5 milliohms or less per joint**, plus a **low-inductance design requirement** and a set of **construction constraints** (direct contact preferred, no jumpers, short wide strap only as a last resort). The RF behaviour is controlled by a *performance* requirement — the bond path must be low enough in impedance, including resonances, to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest — not by a numeric impedance ceiling.

The standard is explicit that the dc number does not bound RF impedance. From Appendix B (§B.3.1, design guidance):

> "The impedance of an acceptable bond may be in the ohms range for RF even though the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms. The resistance is overshadowed by the inductive reactance of the configuration. Any electronic equipment with conductive mounting feet will probably have an inductive reactance greater than 2.5 milliohms at frequencies above 10 megahertz (MHz). RF bonds may be satisfactory with several ohms of impedance; but, when straps are used, even these levels will be quickly exceeded as frequency increases."

That passage is guidance/rationale, not an acceptance criterion, and it deliberately declines to give a number. It is the closest the document comes to an "RF impedance" figure, and it is a qualitative statement that **several ohms may be satisfactory** — not a maximum, and not tied to a frequency.

## 2. Ask 1 in detail — why no number exists

Three separate reasons the requested value does not exist:

1. **The requirement quantity is dc resistance, not RF impedance.** The only numeric bond-resistance value associated with Class R is 2.5 mΩ dc. It is measured with a micro-ohmmeter / four-wire Kelvin method (this is how 4003A Class R conformance is actually verified in published NASA test work — see §6).
2. **No frequency is stated for any impedance limit.** The only frequency figure in the document near this subject is the 10 MHz used in the Appendix B example above — and it is used to illustrate that a 2.5 mΩ-compliant bond is already dominated by inductive reactance there, not to define a limit at 10 MHz.
3. **The RF requirement is written as a performance outcome, not a number.** See §3, item 6.

If a designer needs a number to put on a drawing, it has to be *derived by the program* from the EMC and antenna requirements (method in §7). NASA-STD-4003A will not supply it.

## 3. Ask 2 in detail — the actual Class R requirement set

| # | Attribute | NASA-STD-4003A requirement for Class R | Nature |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Purpose / definition | "Requires low RF impedance at high frequency. Direct contact preferred. No jumpers. Short, wide strap may be used as last resort." (Table 1) | Class definition + construction constraint |
| 2 | DC bond resistance | "Bonding resistance requirement, 2.5 milliohms or less. Low inductance required." (Table 1) | **Numeric requirement — the only one** |
| 3 | Inductance | "Low inductance required" (Table 1); "the bond should be low inductance" (App. B, §B.3.1) | Requirement (qualitative) |
| 4 | Frequency classification | FREQ. REQT. = **High** (relative to the other classes) | Classification, not a band edge |
| 5 | Current classification | CURRENT REQT. = **Low** (relative to the other classes) | Classification, not a current value |
| 6 | System-level impedance | The path to structure and the joints in it "shall be designed such that the inductance and overall impedance including resonances are low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest." | Performance requirement — verified by analysis/test, no numeric ceiling |
| 7 | Strap geometry (if a strap is unavoidable) | "strap length should always be limited to a length to width ratio of 5 to 1" (App. B) | Design rule |
| 8 | Joint scope | The 2.5 mΩ applies **across each joint**, not to the sum of a multi-joint path. A path with n joints can therefore present up to ~n × 2.5 mΩ dc while every joint is compliant. | Requirement scope |
| 9 | Antenna / groundplane bonds | Return path to vehicle structure "that exhibits a dc resistance no greater than 2.5 milliohms"; counterpoise/groundplane 1/4 wavelength in radius over the antenna's operating band for monopole or half-loop antennas on composite OML surfaces. | Requirement (dc) + geometric requirement |
| 10 | Multi-purpose bonds | Where Class R and another class both apply, the bond must satisfy the strictest combination. Appendix B example: equipment powered from the system supply needs "Class R bonding for RF and Class H bonding for fault current" — low inductance with ≤ 2.5 mΩ dc **and** enough contact area for the maximum fault current. | Requirement |
| 11 | RF impedance ceiling | **None stated.** | No requirement |

Supporting text from the standard's own worked example (Appendix B, §B.3.1):

> "…it would require Class R bonding for RF and Class H bonding for fault current protection. Since both classes are applicable, the bond should be low inductance with no more than 2.5 milliohms dc resistance for Class R, and the contact area should be adequate to carry the maximum fault current that could occur for Class H."

And the antenna paragraph:

> "…should be installed with a low impedance return path to vehicle structure that exhibits a dc resistance no greater than 2.5 milliohms, so that antenna fields are not attenuated by poorly conductive composite material."

## 4. Class taxonomy context (why the Class R column says what it says)

Table 1 is a matrix of bond classes against four attributes — purpose, dc bond resistance requirement, frequency requirement, and current requirement. Reading the matrix as a whole:

- The class with **2.5 mΩ dc, low inductance required, FREQ REQT = High, CURRENT REQT = Low** is Class R. This is confirmed independently by Appendix B §B.3.1 ("no more than 2.5 milliohms dc resistance for Class R") and by published NASA test work applying 4003A (§6).
- Class R sits between the lightning/static classes (low frequency, high current, resistance depending on current or 0.1 Ω) and the fault-current class (high current, high frequency, joint voltage ≤ 500 V, low inductance). That is why Class R's defining characteristic is *inductance*, not resistance: at RF the geometry dominates.
- Do not assume the class letter maps to a resistance value by any rule of thumb. The values in Table 1 are per-class and must be read from the table.

## 5. Normative vs. informative — important for a designer writing a spec

- **Normative:** the Class R entry in Table 1 (2.5 mΩ dc, low inductance, direct contact, no jumpers, strap as last resort) and the system-level "impedance including resonances… low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest" requirement.
- **Informative/guidance:** Appendix B's "several ohms of impedance" statement and the 5:1 strap rule. These explain *why* the requirement is written as it is and give design direction, but they are not acceptance criteria. A designer cannot cite "several ohms" as a pass/fail limit, and equally cannot be failed for exceeding it if the EMC performance requirement is met by other means.
- **Neither** the normative nor the informative text gives a maximum impedance in ohms at a stated frequency.

## 6. How compliance with Class R is actually demonstrated

The verifiable, numeric part of Class R is the dc resistance. Practice in published NASA bonding test work (NTRS 20140008725, connector/backshell salt-fog qualification for SLS) is:

- **Method:** four-probe Kelvin measurement with a calibrated micro-ohmmeter, taken metal-to-metal across the joint under test, before and after environmental exposure.
- **Criterion applied:** "Per requirements in NASA-STD-4003A, the electrical resistance must not exceed 2.5 mΩ" and "conformance to the class R bonding requirements of NASA-STD-4003A of < 2.5 mΩ."
- **Environmental sequencing:** measurements taken pre-exposure and post-exposure (168 h ASTM B117 salt fog in that program) to show the bond does not degrade out of compliance. This is the practical way the "low inductance / low RF impedance" intent is protected against corrosion-driven resistance growth.

The RF/inductance portion is verified by **analysis** of the as-built geometry (see §7) plus, where the program requires it, EMC testing to the applicable MIL-STD-461 or program EMC control plan limits — not by a bond-impedance measurement against a standard-supplied number, because no such number exists.

## 7. Converting this into a usable, program-specific RF impedance requirement

Since the standard gives no number, the program must derive one. A defensible procedure:

**Step 1 — Start from the dc floor.** Specify "dc resistance across each Class R joint ≤ 2.5 mΩ, measured four-wire Kelvin." This is non-negotiable and comes straight from the standard.

**Step 2 — Bound the geometry, not the impedance.** Specify direct metal-to-metal contact as the primary configuration. Where a strap is unavoidable, specify length:width ≤ 5:1 per Appendix B, and specify the maximum strap length explicitly (the standard's rule alone permits a very long strap if it is proportionally wide, which is not what you want at high frequency).

**Step 3 — Compute the reactance of the worst-case allowed geometry at the highest frequency of interest.** For a straight rectangular strap (length l, width w, thickness h; l ≫ w, h):

  L(µH) = 0.002 · l · [ ln( 2l / (w + h) ) + 0.5 + 0.2235 · (w + h) / l ]   (l, w, h in cm)

  then Z ≈ √(R² + (2πfL)²) ≈ 2πfL for any realistic bond.

Worked examples (both compliant with the 5:1 rule):

| Geometry | L | X @ 1 MHz | X @ 10 MHz | X @ 100 MHz |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 mm × 25 mm × 1 mm strap (4:1) | ≈ 52 nH | 0.33 Ω | 3.3 Ω | 33 Ω |
| 50 mm × 25 mm × 1 mm strap (2:1) | ≈ 20 nH | 0.12 Ω | 1.2 Ω | 12 Ω |
| Direct clamped contact (overlap only) | ≈ 0.1–1 nH | < 0.01 Ω | < 0.07 Ω | < 0.7 Ω |

These numbers are consistent with the standard's own guidance that RF bonds "may be satisfactory with several ohms of impedance" and that straps "quickly exceed" that as frequency rises — and they show concretely why a single ohm value in the standard would be meaningless: the same compliant joint is 0.33 Ω at 1 MHz and 33 Ω at 100 MHz.

**Step 4 — Set the acceptance number from the mission requirement, not from the bond.** Derive Z_max from whichever of these governs:

- **Shield termination / EMI:** the bond is one element of a shield-to-structure transfer-impedance budget. Allocate the bond a fraction (commonly 10 % or less) of the total allowable transfer impedance at the highest frequency of concern.
- **Antenna groundplane / counterpoise:** allocate an allowable ground-loss resistance/reactance consistent with the antenna efficiency and pattern budget; the standard's 2.5 mΩ dc and quarter-wavelength counterpoise radius are the starting points.
- **Common-impedance coupling / ground shift:** bound the bond reactance so that the voltage developed across it by the largest expected RF current stays below the susceptibility threshold of the victim circuit.

**Step 5 — Write it as a derived requirement** in the program's bonding or EMC control document, e.g.:

> "Class R bond impedance shall not exceed Z_max = [derived value] Ω at frequencies up to f_max = [derived value], and dc resistance shall not exceed 2.5 mΩ per joint. Compliance shall be shown by four-wire Kelvin dc measurement plus inductance calculation of the as-built geometry; where the derived Z_max is not met by calculation, direct metal-to-metal contact shall be used in place of a strap."

That is the correct engineering answer to the designer's real question: the standard gives the floor and the design rules, the program must supply the impedance ceiling.

## 8. Common misconceptions to correct with the designer

1. **"4003A says Class R is X ohms at Y MHz."** No. 4003A says ≤ 2.5 mΩ dc, low inductance, direct contact, no jumpers. No ohms-at-a-frequency figure exists.
2. **"2.5 mΩ is the RF impedance limit."** No — 2.5 mΩ is dc. The standard warns in Appendix B that a bond can be ≤ 2.5 mΩ dc and already be inductive well above 2.5 mΩ of reactance at 10 MHz and above.
3. **"A bond that passes the micro-ohmmeter test is a good RF bond."** The 2003 predecessor text says it directly: "The 2.5-milliohm dc resistance requirement is good for a standard, but one should not assume a good RF bond exists just because the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms."
4. **"The 2.5 mΩ applies to the whole path."** It applies per joint. Count the joints.
5. **"MIL-STD-461 will give me the number."** It will not; 461 sets emissions and susceptibility limits, not bond impedance. The bond impedance budget must be derived from the 461 limits or the program EMC plan.
6. **"Any strap is fine as long as it's short."** The standard's rule is length:width ≤ 5:1, and a strap is a last resort after direct contact, not a default.

## 9. What to check before locking this into a program

- **Contractually invoked revision.** The question names 4003A. The NASA Technical Standards System lists NASA-STD-4003A with Change 1, revalidated 13 March 2026. The Class R 2.5 mΩ value and the Appendix B language are identical in the base 4003A and the Change 1 text as fetched, so Change 1 does not alter this answer — but the contract's applicable-documents list is what governs, and the program should confirm 4003A (with or without Change 1) is the invoked revision.
- **Predecessor documents.** If the program is older, it may invoke NASA-STD-4003 (2003), which carries the same 2.5 mΩ Class R value and the same guidance. Its §4.3 body text also contains the "impedance including resonances… at the frequencies of interest" performance requirement and the "across each joint" scoping, quoted above. The corresponding 4003A body paragraph was not fully captured in the source excerpts used here, so treat the §4.3 wording as the 2003-predecessor formulation of a requirement that 4003A carries in substance — verify the exact 4003A paragraph number and EBR tag against the controlled copy.
- **Items not verified against the fetched text** (do not quote these as established): the exact 4003A paragraph/EBR number carrying the 2.5 mΩ requirement; the 4003A surface-preparation and finish requirements (bare-metal contact, prohibited finishes, plating callouts); the specified measurement instrument and joint-conditioning procedure; any environmental/aging allowance. These are in the standard but were not in the excerpts available here — read them from the controlled copy before writing them into a work instruction.
- **Program-specific or prime-contractor bonding specifications** may impose a numeric RF impedance that 4003A does not. If the designer's requirement came from somewhere, it came from there, not from 4003A.

## 10. Sources used

- NASA-STD-4003A w/Change 1 (NASA Technical Standards System), Table 1 (Electrical Bond Classes), §4.1, Appendix B §B.3.1 and antenna groundplane paragraph.
- NASA-STD-4003A (base release) — same Class R values and Appendix B text.
- NASA-STD-4003 (8 September 2003) §4.3 — "each joint shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms," "impedance including resonances… at the frequencies of interest," and the caution against assuming an RF bond from a dc measurement.
- NTRS 20140008725 (connector/backshell salt-fog qualification, SLS) — application of "the class R bonding requirements of NASA-STD-4003A of < 2.5 mΩ" with four-probe Kelvin micro-ohmmeter measurements.

question: X39
shape: Oil spill prevention, US EPA (SPCC applicability)
answer:
APPLICABLE RULE
40 CFR Part 112, Spill Prevention, Control, and Countermeasure (SPCC) rule, applies to non-transportation-related onshore facilities that handle oil and could reasonably be expected to discharge oil to navigable waters or adjoining shorelines. The capacity gates are in 40 CFR 112.1(d)(2), with the container-counting rules in 112.1(d)(2)(ii) and the definitions in 112.2.

ASK 1 — THE TWO CAPACITY CEILINGS
A facility remains outside SPCC coverage on capacity grounds only if BOTH of the following are true:

1. Aggregate aboveground oil storage capacity is 1,320 U.S. gallons or less.
2. Aggregate completely buried oil storage capacity is 42,000 U.S. gallons or less.

Equivalently, the facility becomes subject to SPCC if either total is greater than its ceiling:
- aboveground: more than 1,320 U.S. gallons; or
- completely buried: more than 42,000 U.S. gallons.

The ceilings are inclusive: exactly 1,320 gallons aboveground and exactly 42,000 gallons completely buried are outside coverage. One gallon over either ceiling triggers coverage, assuming the other applicability conditions (non-transportation-related facility and reasonable expectation of discharge to navigable waters or adjoining shorelines) are met.

ASK 2 — WHICH ABOVEGROUND CONTAINERS COUNT
Count toward the 1,320-gallon aboveground total:
- Any aboveground oil storage container with a capacity of 55 U.S. gallons or greater. This includes ordinary aboveground tanks and drums.
- Bunkered tanks and partially buried tanks, as defined in 40 CFR 112.2, and containers in vaults. These are treated as aboveground storage containers for Part 112 purposes.
- Containers used for standby storage, seasonal storage, or temporary storage, and any container that is not “permanently closed” as defined in 112.2. An empty or currently unused container still counts if it is not permanently closed.
- Capacity is the container’s shell capacity (maximum volume), not the actual amount of oil normally stored (operational volume).

Do NOT count toward the aboveground total:
- Containers with a storage capacity of less than 55 U.S. gallons.
- Permanently closed containers.
- Motive power containers, as defined in 112.2.
- Hot-mix asphalt and hot-mix asphalt containers.
- Containers for heating oil used solely at a single-family residence.
- Pesticide application equipment and related mix containers.
- Milk and milk product containers and associated piping and appurtenances.
- Containers used exclusively for wastewater treatment, where that facility or part is used exclusively for wastewater treatment and is not used to satisfy any Part 112 requirement.
- Completely buried tanks. These are not part of the aboveground total; they are counted separately against the 42,000-gallon completely buried ceiling.

COMPLETELY BURIED SIDE (for completeness)
Count completely buried tanks toward the 42,000-gallon total. Do not count completely buried tanks and connected underground piping, ancillary equipment, and containment systems that are subject to all technical requirements of 40 CFR Part 280 or 281; nuclear power generation facility underground emergency diesel generator tanks deferred under Part 280 and licensed by and subject to NRC design and quality criteria; permanently closed containers; or containers used exclusively for wastewater treatment.

CALCULATION PROCEDURE
1. Inventory all oil containers at the facility.
2. For each aboveground container, record shell capacity in U.S. gallons. Exclude containers under 55 gallons and the exclusions listed above. Sum the remaining shell capacities. Compare the sum to 1,320 gallons.
3. For each completely buried tank, record shell capacity. Exclude the buried-tank exclusions listed above. Sum the remaining capacities. Compare the sum to 42,000 gallons.
4. If both sums are at or below their ceilings, the facility is outside SPCC coverage on capacity grounds. If either sum exceeds its ceiling, the facility is subject to SPCC on capacity grounds, assuming the non-transportation-related and discharge-potential conditions are also met.

EXAMPLE
A facility has ten 55-gallon drums (550 gallons), one 1,000-gallon aboveground tank, and one 500-gallon aboveground tank. None is excluded. Aboveground total = 550 + 1,000 + 500 = 2,050 gallons. This exceeds 1,320 gallons, so the facility is subject to SPCC on the aboveground side regardless of its buried total.

COMMON CONFLATION TO AVOID
10,000 gallons aggregate aboveground and 5,000 gallons for a single aboveground container are qualified-facility criteria for self-certifying an SPCC Plan under 112.1(g); they are not the SPCC applicability ceilings. The applicability ceilings are 1,320 gallons aboveground and 42,000 gallons completely buried.

question: X42
answer:
IRF540NPbF (Infineon, Rev. 2.1, 2026-07-24) — power dissipation and derating

SOURCE VERIFIED
Document: Infineon IRF540NPbF datasheet, header 'Rev. 2.1, 2026-07-24', revision history entry '2026-07-24 | 2.1 | Update datasheet to Infineon format'. Retrieved from three Infineon-hosted URLs (infineon.com/dgdl/irf540npbf.pdf, infineon.com/dgdl/Infineon-IRF540N-DataSheet-v01_01-EN.pdf, infineon.com/assets/row/public/documents/24/49/infineon-irf540n-datasheet-en.pdf), all with identical content hash sha256 a3fd62a76cc8. Package: TO-220 (the only package variant in this datasheet; TO-220AB, through-hole). Temperature reference for the ratings below is CASE temperature, TC, as printed in the symbol ('PD @ TC = 25 degC').

EXTRACTED VALUES (Absolute Maximum Ratings table, page 1)
  Symbol / Parameter                              Max.      Unit
  PD @ TC = 25 degC  Maximum Power Dissipation   130       W
  Linear Derating Factor                          0.87      W/degC
  (context) ID @ TC = 25 degC                     33        A
  (context) ID @ TC = 100 degC                    23        A
  (context) TJ Operating Junction                   -55 to +175  degC

ASK 1 — Maximum power dissipation at TC = 25 degC
  130 W.
  Condition of validity: TC = 25 degC means the case is held at 25 degC by the thermal design (heatsink), not free-air. This is a package/thermal-limited absolute maximum, not an achievable free-air number (a bare TO-220 in still air is roughly 2 W).

ASK 2 — Linear derating factor
  0.87 W/degC (i.e. 1.15 degC/W, the inverse; equivalent junction-to-case thermal resistance implied by this rating = 150 K / 130 W = 1.154 degC/W).

ASK 3 — Maximum power dissipation permitted at TC = 100 degC
  Linear derating above the 25 degC reference point:
    P(TC) = PD(25 degC) - (derating factor) x (TC - 25 degC)
    P(100 degC) = 130 W - 0.87 W/degC x (100 - 25) degC
                = 130 W - 0.87 x 75 W
                = 130 W - 65.25 W
                = 64.75 W
  Report as 64.75 W; to the two-significant-figure precision of the printed derating factor, 65 W (or 64.8 W to 0.1 W).

VALIDITY WINDOW OF THE LINEAR MODEL (checked, and 100 degC falls inside it)
  Zero-dissipation intercept: TC0 = 25 + 130/0.87 = 174.4 degC, consistent with TJ,max = 175 degC. The 0.87 W/degC figure is itself the rounded form of 130 W / (175 - 25) K = 0.8667 W/degC; using that exact value gives P(100 degC) = 130 - 0.8667 x 75 = 65.0 W. Both results round to 65 W, so the answer is not sensitive to this rounding at the requested precision. Derating applies for 25 degC <= TC <= ~174 degC only; below 25 degC the rating is clamped at 130 W.

DESIGN NOTES / CAVEATS
1. The 64.75 W figure is a die/junction limit referred to case temperature. It is not a free-air rating and not a guarantee of continuous operation: the actual usable dissipation is min(64.75 W at TC = 100 degC, SOA limit from Fig. 8, transient-thermal-impedance limit from Fig. 11 for pulsed duty). Verify against Fig. 8 (Maximum Safe Operating Area) and Fig. 11 at the actual VDS and pulse width.
2. Infineon's product web page for IRF540N lists Ptot,max = 140 W and RthJC,max = 1.1 K/W. Those numbers do not reproduce the datasheet's 130 W / 0.87 W/degC pair (1.1 K/W would give 136 W at TC = 25 degC with TJ = 175 degC). Treat this as a parametric-database inconsistency and use the datasheet values (130 W, 0.87 W/degC), which are the values the request names. If a design margin study is required, use the more conservative datasheet pair.
3. The datasheet does not state whether RthJC is typical or maximum in the thermal table; Fig. 11 is labelled 'Maximum Effective Transient Thermal Impedance'. For worst-case design, derate from 130 W using RthJC = 1.15 degC/W (the value implied by 0.87 W/degC), and add a margin of at least 20-25% on junction temperature.
4. Sibling ratings at TC = 100 degC (ID = 23 A) are set by bond-wire/package current limits, not by the 64.75 W dissipation limit; do not use them interchangeably. At VDS above roughly 2.8 V and 23 A the conduction loss alone exceeds 64.75 W, so the current rating is only meaningful at low VDS.
5. Junction temperature must be confirmed in the application: TJ = TC + P x RthJC. At TC = 100 degC and P = 64.75 W, TJ = 100 + 64.75 x 1.154 = 174.7 degC, i.e. exactly at TJ,max = 175 degC — there is no margin. A practical continuous design target is TJ <= 125-150 degC, which corresponds at TC = 100 degC to roughly 22-43 W, not 64.75 W.

REPRODUCTION PROCEDURE (for verification by a second engineer)
  a. Download the datasheet from any of the three Infineon URLs above; confirm header 'Rev. 2.1, 2026-07-24' and that the revision-history table ends with '2026-07-24 | 2.1'.
  b. Read page 1, Absolute Maximum Ratings: confirm 'PD @TC = 25 degC Maximum Power Dissipation 130 W' and 'Linear Derating Factor 0.87 W/degC'.
  c. Compute P(100) = 130 - 0.87 x (100 - 25) = 64.75 W.
  d. Sanity-check against the datasheet's own thermal data: 130 W / (175 - 25) degC = 0.8667 W/degC ~ 0.87 W/degC, and RthJC = 1/0.87 = 1.15 degC/W.
cautions: The answer gives 64.75 W for ask 3, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.

question: X3
answer:
## 1. Answer

Source of authority: **WHO global air quality guidelines: particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), ozone, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide and carbon monoxide** (WHO, Geneva, 22 September 2021; ISBN 978-92-4-003422-8; 290 pp.; guideline document, not a national/regional standard).

| # | Pollutant | Averaging time | 2021 AQG level |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) | **Sulfur dioxide (SO2)** | **24-hour mean** | **40 µg/m3** |
| (b) | **Nitrogen dioxide (NO2)** | **Annual mean** | **10 µg/m3** |

Both values are as published by WHO; no conversion, rounding or interpolation has been applied. The answer to the enumerated ask (ask 1) is (a) = **40 µg/m3**; part (b) = **10 µg/m3** is given here because the original request asks for it, but it is not carried into the results array since only ask 1 was enumerated as a value ask.

---

## 2. Where these numbers come from (verification trail)

Both figures appear twice in the 2021 guidelines, in two independent tables that cross-check each other:

**(i) Executive-summary table (p. xvii of the guideline PDF), columns = Interim targets … AQG level:**

```
NO2, µg/m3   Annual    40   30   20   –    10
NO2, µg/m3   24-houra  120  50   –    –    25
SO2, µg/m3   24-houra  125  50   –    –    40
CO,  mg/m3   24-houra  7    –    –    –    4
```

**(ii) Table 3.26, "Recommended 2021 AQG levels and 2005 air quality guidelines", p. 135:**

```
NO2, µg/m3   Annual    40   10
NO2, µg/m3   24-houra  –    25
SO2, µg/m3   24-houra  20   40
```
(column 1 = 2005 guidelines, column 2 = 2021 AQG levels — see §3)

Table 3.25 in the same chapter also lists the short-averaging-time guidelines that remain valid from Global update 2005: **NO2 1-hour = 200 µg/m3**, **SO2 10-minute = 500 µg/m3**, **CO 8-hour = 10 mg/m3**, **CO 1-hour = 35 mg/m3**, **CO 15-minute = 100 mg/m3**. These are *not* 2021 AQG levels and must not be quoted as such.

Citation string for downstream use: *WHO global air quality guidelines (2021), Table 3.26, p. 135 (and executive summary, p. xvii).*

---

## 3. Column-order check — why SO2 is 40 and not 20

The 2005→2021 comparison table is a frequent source of error because the 2005 column and the 2021 column sit side by side and OCR/text extraction does not always preserve which is which. Resolving it from rows with independently known values:

| Row (Table 3.26) | Printed pair | 2005 value | 2021 AQG | Conclusion |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PM2.5 annual | 10, 5 | 10 | 5 | 2nd column = 2021 |
| PM2.5 24-h | 25, 15 | 25 | 15 | 2nd column = 2021 |
| PM10 annual | 20, 15 | 20 | 15 | 2nd column = 2021 |
| PM10 24-h | 50, 45 | 50 | 45 | 2nd column = 2021 |
| NO2 annual | 40, 10 | 40 | 10 | 2nd column = 2021 |
| NO2 24-h | –, 25 | (none) | 25 | 2nd column = 2021 |
| **SO2 24-h** | **20, 40** | **20** | **40** | **2nd column = 2021** |

The executive-summary table independently confirms the 2021 column: NO2 annual AQG = 10, NO2 24-h AQG = 25, SO2 24-h AQG = 40.

**Therefore: the 2021 AQG level for the 24-hour mean of SO2 is 40 µg/m3. The value 20 µg/m3 is the superseded 2005 guideline for SO2 24-hour and must not be reported as the 2021 level.** This is the one substantive trap in the question: the SO2 24-hour guideline was *relaxed* (20 → 40 µg/m3) in the 2021 update, whereas almost every other value was tightened — so the usual intuition ("the 2021 number is the lower one") gives the wrong answer here.

Direction of revision, for the record:
- SO2 24-hour: 20 µg/m3 (2005) → **40 µg/m3** (2021) — revised upward.
- NO2 annual: 40 µg/m3 (2005) → **10 µg/m3** (2021) — revised sharply downward.

---

## 4. Interim targets (context; not the AQG level)

WHO publishes interim targets (IT) as a stepped trajectory toward the AQG level. They are *not* guideline levels and should not be substituted for them.

| Pollutant | Averaging time | IT-1 | IT-2 | IT-3 | **AQG level** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SO2 | 24-hour | 125 | 50 | – | **40** |
| NO2 | Annual | 40 | 30 | 20 | **10** |
| NO2 | 24-hour | 120 | 50 | – | **25** |

Consistency check: every interim target is ≥ its corresponding AQG level and the sequence is monotonic toward the AQG (125 > 50 > 40; 40 > 30 > 20 > 10; 120 > 50 > 25). No inversion.

---

## 5. Averaging conventions and footnotes

- The WHO tables attach footnote *a* — "99th percentile (i.e. 3–4 exceedance days per year)" — to the 24-hour averaging times, including SO2 24-hour. In practice this means the SO2 24-hour AQG of 40 µg/m3 is applied to the 99th percentile of daily means over a year, i.e. roughly 3–4 exceedance days per year are tolerated by the metric, rather than demanding zero daily exceedances.
- The annual mean for NO2 (10 µg/m3) is a long-term exposure metric; no exceedance-day allowance applies.
- WHO's own note distinguishes long-term exposure metrics (annual, peak season) from short-term exposure metrics (24-hour, 8-hour). The two rows asked about here span both categories: SO2 24-hour is short-term; NO2 annual is long-term.
- The 2021 update did **not** set a SO2 annual mean AQG and did not set an SO2 1-hour AQG; the 2005 10-minute value (500 µg/m3) remains valid. Likewise the 2005 NO2 1-hour value (200 µg/m3) remains valid.

---

## 6. Units

- Values are stated by WHO in **µg/m3** and are reported here exactly as published; no conversion is needed or performed.
- WHO 2021 does not express the AQG levels in ppb. If a ppb figure is needed for a downstream comparison (e.g. against an instrument reading), convert at 25 °C and 101.325 kPa using molar volume 24.45 L/mol:
  - SO2 (MW 64.066): 40 µg/m3 × 24.45 / 64.066 ≈ **15.3 ppb**
  - NO2 (MW 46.0055): 10 µg/m3 × 24.45 / 46.0055 ≈ **5.3 ppb**
  These ppb figures are informative only and are not WHO guideline values; the authoritative statement is in µg/m3. Conversion at a different reference temperature/pressure will shift them (e.g. at 0 °C, 22.4 L/mol: SO2 ≈ 14.0 ppb, NO2 ≈ 4.9 ppb).
- Note the CO row in the same WHO tables is in **mg/m3**, not µg/m3 — a common transcription error when copying whole tables.

---

## 7. Scope boundaries (what this answer is and is not)

- It reports the **final AQG levels** only; interim targets are given in §4 for context but are not the answer.
- It uses the **WHO 2021 global** guidelines, not EU limit values, US EPA NAAQS, or national standards; those differ materially (e.g. the EU limit value for NO2 annual mean is 40 µg/m3, four times the WHO 2021 AQG level of 10).
- It requires no project-specific data, monitoring results or compliance determination.
- If a different averaging period was actually intended for either pollutant (e.g. SO2 10-minute, NO2 1-hour or NO2 24-hour), the correct values are: SO2 10-minute 500 µg/m3 (2005, retained); NO2 1-hour 200 µg/m3 (2005, retained); NO2 24-hour 25 µg/m3 (2021).

---

## 8. Quick-reference summary block

```
WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines, 2021 update (ISBN 978-92-4-003422-8)

SO2  24-hour mean  AQG level = 40 µg/m3   (IT-1 125, IT-2 50; 2005 value was 20)
NO2  annual mean   AQG level = 10 µg/m3   (IT-1 40, IT-2 30, IT-3 20; 2005 value was 40)

Retained from 2005 and still valid: SO2 10-min 500 µg/m3; NO2 1-hour 200 µg/m3
Not to be confused with: interim targets (above), EU/EPA standards, or the 2005 column.
```

question: X6
answer:
# REACH Article 33 consumer SVHC enquiry — operative answers and response procedure

## 1. The three answers

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Above what concentration in the article does the retailer's duty to answer arise? | **0.1 % w/w** of the article — and strictly *above* 0.1 %. At exactly 0.1 % the duty is not triggered. |
| 2 | Within how many days must it answer? | **45 days** from receipt of the consumer's request. |
| 3 | May it charge for the answer? | **No.** The information must be provided free of charge. |

## 2. Legal basis (verbatim)

REACH, Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006, Article 33(2):

> 'On request by a consumer any supplier of an article containing a substance meeting the criteria in Article 57 and identified in accordance with Article 59(1) in a concentration above 0,1 % weight by weight (w/w) shall provide the consumer with sufficient information, available to the supplier, to allow safe use of the article including, as a minimum, the name of that substance.
> The relevant information shall be provided, free of charge, within 45 days of receipt of the request.'

All three answers come from that single subparagraph. The text is stable across the consolidated versions checked (2015-05-13, 2016-03-08, 2021-08-25); no amendment has altered the 0.1 % figure, the 45-day period or the free-of-charge rule.

## 3. Scope conditions that must hold for the duty to bite

The three answers above are unconditional; whether the duty applies to a *particular* enquiry depends on four conditions. All four must be checked and recorded:

1. **The product is an article** within the meaning of Article 3(3) REACH — an object which during production is given a special shape, surface or design determining its function to a greater degree than its chemical composition. A liquid, powder, gel or other unbounded product is a substance or mixture, and Article 33 does not apply to it (Article 31 / safety data sheet rules apply instead, with their own thresholds of 1 % w/w for non-gaseous and 0.2 % v/v for gaseous mixtures under Article 31(3) — these are *not* the article threshold and must not be quoted to the consumer).
2. **The substance is on the candidate list** (Article 59(1)) **on the date of the request**. Check the ECHA candidate list as at that date and record the version consulted. A substance listed only after the request does not retroactively create a duty for that request; a substance listed before it does, irrespective of when the article was manufactured.
3. **The retailer is a supplier of the article.** Article 3(14) defines a distributor as including a retailer; a retailer that sells or otherwise makes the article available is a supplier for Article 33 purposes. The duty is not limited to the manufacturer or importer, and a retailer cannot deflect it by saying it is 'only a shop'.
4. **The concentration in the article exceeds 0.1 % w/w.** See section 4.

If condition 1, 2 or 4 fails, the Article 33(2) duty does not arise — but a reply is still good practice and may be required by national consumer-protection law, so answer anyway, explaining why no SVHC disclosure obligation applies.

## 4. How the 0.1 % is measured

Concentration = (mass of the candidate-list substance / mass of the article) x 100, expressed in weight by weight.

- The denominator is the **article as placed on the market**, not a homogeneous material, a coating, a component part or the packaging (unless the packaging is itself a separate article).
- For a **complex object** (e.g. a bicycle, a chair, an appliance), the prevailing enforcement approach, following ECHA's Guidance on requirements for substances in articles, is to treat the object as an assembly of articles and to test the threshold **article by article**; if any constituent article exceeds 0.1 % w/w, the duty is triggered for that object. Record which constituent article triggered the duty.
- **Boundary rule:** strictly greater than 0.1 %. A concentration of exactly 0.1 % does not trigger the duty; a concentration of 0.1 % plus any measurable increment does. Where measurement uncertainty straddles the boundary, treat the duty as triggered and answer — the cost of answering is trivial, the cost of wrongly refusing is enforcement exposure.
- **Worked check:** a 2 kg article contains 2 g of the substance. 2 g / 2000 g = 0.001 = 0.1 % — exactly at the line, so the duty is **not** triggered; 2.1 g (0.105 %) would trigger it.
- The retailer does **not** have to disclose the concentration figure itself. The legal minimum is the **name of the substance** plus enough information, available to the supplier, to allow safe use. Concentration is not a mandatory disclosure item, so commercial-confidentiality concerns about the percentage are not a ground for refusing the name.

## 5. The 45-day clock

- It runs from **receipt of the request by the retailer**, not from the date the consumer thought about asking, not from the date the retailer's head office forwards it, and not from the date the upstream supplier replies.
- There is **no form requirement**: an oral question at the counter, a phone call, an email or a web form all start the clock. Any employee acting for the retailer can receive it.
- Counting: calendar days. Under the general EU time-limit rules (Regulation (EEC, Euratom) No 1182/71) the day of receipt is not counted and the period expires at the end of the 45th day, rolling to the next working day if that day is a public holiday, Saturday or Sunday. **Do not rely on the roll-over** — build the internal plan to finish early (section 6).
- The clock is **not suspended** while the retailer chases its own supplier. The obligation is to give the information *available to the supplier*; a retailer that has none must still respond within 45 days with what it has and an honest statement of position, and must not simply let the deadline pass.
- **Lever to get the data:** Article 33(1) obliges the upstream supplier to provide *the retailer* (as recipient of the article) with sufficient information, including at minimum the substance name, where the 0.1 % threshold is exceeded. Cite Article 33(1) when requesting data from the supplier or importer.

## 6. Response procedure

| Step | Timing (day 0 = receipt) | Action |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Day 0 | Log the request: date and time received, channel, consumer identity and contact, exact product and batch/order reference. The log entry is the evidence of when the 45 days started. |
| 2 | Day 0–5 | Acknowledge in writing, confirm the product identified, and state that a substantive answer will follow. Acknowledging does not stop the clock but protects against 'no reply' findings. |
| 3 | Day 1–5 | Establish the product is an article. Pull the technical file / bill of materials / supplier declarations. Check the ECHA candidate list as at the request date for each substance flagged. |
| 4 | Day 5 | If in-house data is insufficient, issue a written request to the upstream supplier/importer citing Article 33(1), asking for: substance name, whether concentration exceeds 0.1 % w/w, and safe-use information. Set them a **day 25** deadline. |
| 5 | Day 25–30 | Draft the answer (template in section 7). Choose the correct branch: above threshold / at or below threshold / genuinely unknown after reasonable enquiry. |
| 6 | Day 30–40 | Internal review and sign-off (compliance + legal). Buffer for late upstream data. |
| 7 | **Day 40** | Send. Internal hard stop, five days inside the legal deadline. |
| 8 | Day 45 | **Legal deadline.** Any answer sent after this date is a breach. |
| 9 | After sending | File the request, the candidate-list version consulted, the upstream correspondence and the answer sent. Retain per the member state's enforcement practice; a 3-year retention is a prudent default. |

Every milestone above sits inside the 45-day limit: 5 < 25 < 30 < 40 < 45.

## 7. Answer-letter template

> Dear [consumer],
> Thank you for your enquiry of [date] about [product, order reference], received by us on [date].
> [Branch A — above threshold] The product is an article within the meaning of Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 (REACH). It contains [substance name], which is on the candidate list of substances of very high concern, in a concentration above 0.1 % weight by weight. Information relevant to safe use: [safe-use information available to us]. This information is provided free of charge in accordance with Article 33(2) of REACH.
> [Branch B — at or below threshold] The product is an article within the meaning of REACH. [Substance] is on the candidate list, but on the basis of the information available to us it is not present in the article in a concentration above 0.1 % weight by weight, so the Article 33(2) disclosure duty does not arise. [State the basis: supplier declaration, test report, date.]
> [Branch C — unknown] The product is an article within the meaning of REACH. We have asked our supplier for confirmation whether [substance] is present above 0.1 % weight by weight and will write to you again as soon as we have it. In the meantime, the information available to us is: [whatever is held].
> Yours sincerely, [name, function]

Branch C is a holding answer, not a discharge of the obligation: it must be followed by a substantive answer **within the same 45-day window**. If the supplier does not reply in time, send Branch C's substance as the final answer within 45 days and record the supplier's failure.

## 8. The fee question in practice

Article 33(2) says the information 'shall be provided, free of charge'. Consequences:

- No administration fee, handling fee, research fee, postage fee, photocopying fee or 'analysis' fee may be charged.
- The answer may not be conditioned on a purchase, on registering an account, on joining a loyalty scheme, or on the consumer invoking a formal procedure.
- A third party (e.g. an online marketplace or a fulfilment provider) acting for the retailer may not charge either.
- Charging, or refusing to answer pending payment, is a breach of Article 33(2) and exposes the retailer to the member state's enforcement measures and penalties, which vary by member state.

## 9. Edge cases

- **Substance not on the candidate list at the request date:** no Article 33(2) duty. Say so and give the date of the list version checked.
- **Product is a mixture, not an article** (e.g. a cleaning fluid, a paint): Article 33 does not apply; the safety data sheet regime under Article 31 applies, with its own thresholds. Redirect the answer accordingly.
- **Retailer is a pure intermediary that never takes physical possession** (e.g. drop-shipping marketplace): it may still be 'placing on the market' and therefore a supplier. Do not assume exemption; get the upstream Article 33(1) declaration.
- **Confidential business information:** no ground to withhold the substance name from a consumer. The concentration figure need not be given.
- **Overlapping duties:** Article 7(2) notification to ECHA and SCIP notification under Article 9(1)(i) of the Waste Framework Directive use the same 0.1 % w/w trigger and are separate obligations; satisfying them does not satisfy Article 33(2), and vice versa. SCIP data can be a useful internal source for the answer.
- **Request predates a candidate-list addition:** no duty for that request; a fresh request after listing does trigger it.

## 10. Limits of this analysis

This is a compliance analysis, not legal advice. It states the position under the REACH text as consolidated at 2021-08-25. Two caveats: (a) national enforcement practice and consumer-protection law vary by member state and may add duties, never remove them; (b) the Commission's pending proposal to revise REACH would introduce a concentration limit factor that could vary the effective threshold for certain articles — before answering, confirm the version of the Regulation in force at the date of the request. A lawyer should be consulted before the retailer refuses an enquiry or relies on a below-threshold finding.

question: X9
shape: EU RoHS (restriction of hazardous substances in electrical equipment)
answer:
ANSWERS

1. Number of restricted substances in Annex II: 10 (ten entries).
2. The entry with a maximum concentration of 0,01 % by weight in homogeneous materials: Cadmium — and it is the only one.
3. Date from which the restriction on DEHP, BBP, DBP and DIBP applies to medical devices: 22 July 2021.

---

1. ANNEX II AS CURRENTLY CONSOLIDATED (VERBATIM CONTENT)

Heading: 'ANNEX II — Restricted substances referred to in Article 4(1) and maximum concentration values tolerated by weight in homogeneous materials'.

| # | Restricted substance | Max. concentration by weight in homogeneous materials |
|---|----------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| 1 | Lead | 0,1 % |
| 2 | Mercury | 0,1 % |
| 3 | Cadmium | 0,01 % |
| 4 | Hexavalent chromium | 0,1 % |
| 5 | Polybrominated biphenyls (PBB) | 0,1 % |
| 6 | Polybrominated diphenyl ethers (PBDE) | 0,1 % |
| 7 | Bis(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP) | 0,1 % |
| 8 | Butyl benzyl phthalate (BBP) | 0,1 % |
| 9 | Dibutyl phthalate (DBP) | 0,1 % |
| 10 | Diisobutyl phthalate (DIBP) | 0,1 % |

Count = 10 rows. Nine entries at 0,1 %; one entry at 0,01 %.

Provenance of this Annex text: substituted in its entirety by Commission Delegated Directive (EU) 2015/863 of 31 March 2015 amending Annex II to Directive 2011/65/EU as regards the list of restricted substances (OJ L 137, 4.6.2015, p. 10). The consolidated text marks this substitution '▼M29'.

Note on the word 'substances' (flagged, not resolved silently): the count of 10 is the count of Annex II entries. PBB (entry 5) and PBDE (entry 6) are substance families, not single congeners; if a reader counted individually named chemical species the number would be higher. For RoHS compliance purposes the operative count is the entry count, 10, because Article 4(1) prohibits the substances 'listed in Annex II' and the maximum values are set per entry. Answer stated: 10.

---

2. THE 0,01 % ENTRY

Cadmium is the sole Annex II entry whose maximum tolerated concentration is 0,01 % by weight in homogeneous materials. Every other entry — lead, mercury, hexavalent chromium, PBB, PBDE, DEHP, BBP, DBP, DIBP — is set at 0,1 %.

Two precision points that matter in practice:
- The 0,01 % figure is cadmium-specific. It is NOT a general RoHS threshold, and it must not be applied to any other Annex II substance.
- The limit is expressed 'by weight in homogeneous materials' (Article 4(1) read with Article 4(2)), i.e. it is assessed per homogeneous material, not per article, component or total device mass. A homogeneous material is a material of uniform composition that cannot be mechanically disjointed into different materials.

---

3. THE DATE FOR DEHP, BBP, DBP AND DIBP IN MEDICAL DEVICES

Verbatim from Annex II, first transitional paragraph:

'The restriction of DEHP, BBP, DBP and DIBP shall apply to medical devices, including in vitro medical devices, and monitoring and control instruments, including industrial monitoring and control instruments, from 22 July 2021.'

Answer: 22 July 2021. It covers medical devices including in vitro medical devices, and (in the same sentence) monitoring and control instruments including industrial monitoring and control instruments.

Associated provisions in the same Annex, stated so the 2021 date is not confused with them:
- 22 July 2019 — the date from which the four phthalates are restricted in EEE generally (all other categories).
- Carve-out: the restriction does not apply to cables or spare parts for the repair, reuse, updating of functionalities or upgrading of capacity of EEE placed on the market before 22 July 2019, nor of medical devices (incl. IVD) and monitoring and control instruments (incl. industrial) placed on the market before 22 July 2021.
- Toys: the restriction of DEHP, BBP and DBP does not apply to toys already subject to that restriction through entry 51 of Annex XVII to Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 (REACH).

Distinguish from Article 4(3) dates (a frequent source of error): Article 4(3) provides that paragraph 1 applies to medical devices and monitoring and control instruments placed on the market from 22 July 2014, to in vitro diagnostic medical devices from 22 July 2016, and to industrial monitoring and control instruments from 22 July 2017. Those dates govern the extension of the ORIGINAL six substances (lead, mercury, cadmium, hexavalent chromium, PBB, PBDE) to those product categories. They are not the date for the four phthalates; the phthalates date is 22 July 2021, set in Annex II itself. Both statements are true and they answer different questions.

---

4. VERSION PINNING AND SOURCE RELIABILITY

Versions actually inspected:
- EUR-Lex consolidated text of Directive 2011/65/EU, ELI http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2011/65/2025-01-01 (CELEX consolidation 02011L0065), Annex II marked '▼M29' — shows the same 10 entries and the same 22 July 2021 sentence.
- Point-in-time UK rendering of the EU text at 31/12/2020 (legislation.gov.uk, EU-derived text, which carries the F1 = 2015/863 substitution note) — identical 10 entries and identical transitional wording.
- EUR-Lex act page for CELEX 32011L0065, which lists consolidated versions including 01/01/2025 and 01/07/2026 and shows a current consolidated version of 01/07/2026.

Conclusion on stability: across every version I could inspect, the Annex II substance list is unchanged (10 entries) and the phthalate/medical-device date is unchanged (22 July 2021). No amendment adding or removing an Annex II substance after Delegated Directive (EU) 2015/863 is evidenced in the material inspected; post-2015 amending acts to Directive 2011/65/EU have operated on the exemption Annexes (III and IV), not on the Annex II substance list.

Citation caution for compliance use: EUR-Lex consolidated texts are informational and do not have legal force; the authoritative sources are the Official Journal text of Directive 2011/65/EU (OJ L 174, 1.7.2011, p. 88) as amended, and Delegated Directive (EU) 2015/863 (OJ L 137, 4.6.2015, p. 10). Any declaration of conformity or technical file should cite the OJ acts, with the consolidated version used noted for traceability.

---

5. WHAT THIS ANSWER DOES NOT SAY (scope boundaries)

- It does not say the ten substances can never be present. Annexes III and IV list applications exempted from the Article 4(1) restriction (Annex IV specifically for medical devices and monitoring and control instruments). An exemption, where applicable, permits exceedance of the Annex II maximum for that specific application.
- It does not address REACH, the Medical Devices Regulation (EU) 2017/745, or national implementing law. The 22 July 2021 date is the date in the RoHS instrument itself and does not depend on any national transposition date; 'medical devices' here is the RoHS-defined scope, which expressly includes in vitro medical devices.
- It does not resolve the PBB/PBDE congener-counting question; it states the entry count.

---

6. VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (repeatable)

1. Open the consolidated text of Directive 2011/65/EU on EUR-Lex and pin the consolidation date you are using (record the ELI, e.g. .../2011/65/2025-01-01).
2. Go to Annex II. Confirm the heading reads 'Restricted substances referred to in Article 4(1) and maximum concentration values tolerated by weight in homogeneous materials' and that the substitution note points to Delegated Directive (EU) 2015/863.
3. Count the listed entries. Expected: 10.
4. Scan the bracketed percentages. Expected: exactly one at 0,01 % — cadmium; nine at 0,1 %.
5. Read the first transitional paragraph under the list. Expected: '... shall apply to medical devices, including in vitro medical devices, and monitoring and control instruments, including industrial monitoring and control instruments, from 22 July 2021.'
6. If any of steps 3–5 differs from the above, a newer amendment has changed Annex II: re-answer from the newer text and cite the amending act. Do not carry these three values forward unverified.

---

7. ASSUMPTIONS RECORDED

- 'Restricted substances' = the entries listed in Annex II, counted as entries.
- 'Currently consolidated' = the latest consolidation available on EUR-Lex at the time of answering; the answer is version-stable across the consolidations inspected, so the exact pin does not change any of the three values.
- The 0,01 % question is read as asking which single Annex II entry carries that limit (answer: cadmium), not as asking for a general threshold.
- The date is taken from Annex II's own transitional wording as incorporated into the consolidated text, not from any national transposition measure.

question: X12
shape: International radioactive material transport requirements (IAEA SSR-6 Rev. 2)
answer:
Under IAEA SSR-6 (Rev. 1), the TI of a freight container used as packaging is determined by para. 523:

1. Measure the maximum dose rate at 1 m from the external surfaces: D = 0.08 mSv/h.
2. Multiply by 100: 0.08 x 100 = 8.0.
3. Apply the Table 7 multiplication factor for tanks, freight containers used as packaging and unpackaged LSA-I/SCO-I/SCO-III. Table 7 uses the largest cross-sectional area of the load:
   - size of load <= 1 m2: factor 1
   - 1 m2 < size of load <= 5 m2: factor 2
   - 5 m2 < size of load <= 20 m2: factor 3
   - 20 m2 < size of load: factor 10
   The stated largest cross-sectional area is 3 m2, so the factor is 2.
4. TI = 8.0 x 2 = 16.0.
5. Round up to the first decimal place as required by para. 523: 16.0 remains 16.0.

Therefore the assigned transport index is TI = 16.0.

Limit check: because the freight container used as packaging is not under exclusive use, SSR-6 para. 526(b) applies: the TI of any freight container used as packaging shall not exceed 50. The assigned TI is 16.0, and 16.0 <= 50, so the TI is within the applicable limit.

Verdict: yes, TI = 16.0 is within the non-exclusive-use limit of 50 for a freight container used as packaging.

question: X15
answer:
# WCAG 2.2 pointer-target size requirements

Source of record: **Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2**, W3C Recommendation, 5 October 2023 — https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/ — together with the informative Understanding documents for SC 2.5.8 and SC 2.5.5. All figures below are quoted from the normative text of the Recommendation.

## Answers at a glance

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Level AA criterion setting a minimum pointer-target size | **Success Criterion 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)** (Level AA) — new in WCAG 2.2 |
| 2 | That minimum size | **24 by 24 CSS pixels** (i.e. 24 CSS px per side) |
| 3 | Diameter of the circle used by its spacing exception | **24 CSS pixels** |
| 4 | Size required by the Level AAA 'Target Size (Enhanced)' criterion | **44 by 44 CSS pixels** (SC 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced), Level AAA) |

## 1. The Level AA criterion

**Success Criterion 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)**, under Guideline 2.5 Input Modalities, conformance level **AA**. It is one of the success criteria newly introduced in WCAG 2.2 (there was no target-size success criterion in WCAG 2.1; the AAA 'Target Size (Enhanced)' criterion 2.5.5 originated in WCAG 2.1).

Normative text as published in the Recommendation:

> **2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum):** The size of the target for pointer inputs is at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, except when:
> - **Spacing:** Undersized targets (those less than 24 by 24 CSS pixels) are positioned so that if a 24 CSS pixel diameter circle is centered on the bounding box of each, the circles do not intersect another target or the circle for another undersized target;
> - **Equivalent:** The function can be achieved through a different control on the same page that meets this criterion;
> - **Inline:** The target is in a sentence or its size is otherwise constrained by the line-height of non-target text;
> - **User Agent Control:** The size of the target is determined by the user agent and is not modified by the author;
> - **Essential:** A particular presentation of the target is essential or is legally required for the information being conveyed.

Note that 2.5.8 has **five** exceptions in the published Recommendation. The spacing exception is only one of them; a target below 24 by 24 CSS pixels can conform via any one of the five.

## 2. The minimum size: 24 by 24 CSS pixels

- Per-side minimum: **24 CSS pixels**; the criterion is expressed as a 24 × 24 CSS pixel bounding box.
- 'CSS pixel' is the WCAG-defined reference pixel (CSS Values and Units Module Level 3), not a device pixel and not a physical measurement.
- Targets **at or above** 24 by 24 CSS pixels pass outright; the exceptions only need to be considered for targets **below** 24 by 24 CSS pixels ('undersized targets').

## 3. The spacing exception's circle: 24 CSS pixel diameter

The spacing test is geometric and uses a **circle of 24 CSS pixels diameter** (radius 12 CSS pixels):

1. Take each undersized target (one smaller than 24 × 24 CSS pixels) and center a 24 CSS pixel diameter circle on its bounding box.
2. Repeat for every adjacent target, and for every adjacent undersized target's circle.
3. The exception is met if that circle **does not intersect** another target or the circle of another undersized target.

Worked example from the Understanding document (Understanding SC 2.5.8, Figure 5): a horizontal row of six 20 × 20 CSS pixel icon buttons **passes** with 4 CSS pixels of space between them (the circles clear each other), and **fails** with no space between them (the circles intersect). The same targets at 24 × 24 CSS pixels pass the criterion directly, without needing the exception.

The circle diameter (24 CSS px) is deliberately equal to the minimum target size (24 CSS px): undersized targets must buy back the deficit with spacing.

## 4. The Level AAA enhanced size: 44 by 44 CSS pixels

**Success Criterion 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced)** (Level AAA):

> The size of the target for pointer inputs is at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels except when: **Equivalent** (an equivalent link or control on the same page is at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels); **Inline** (the target is in a sentence or block of text); **User Agent Control** (the size is determined by the user agent and not modified by the author); **Essential** (a particular presentation is essential to the information being conveyed).

- 2.5.5 has **no spacing exception** — the 24 CSS pixel circle test belongs only to 2.5.8. Do not apply the circle test when evaluating against 2.5.5.
- The two thresholds are explicitly reconciled in the Understanding document for 2.5.8: '...the Working Group settled on the smaller measure of 24 by 24 CSS pixels for the "(Minimum)" version of this criterion, while 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced) uses the larger 44 by 44 CSS pixel measure as its threshold size.'
- Sufficient technique for 2.5.5: **C44: Using CSS to ensure targets are at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels**; corresponding failure: target less than 44 by 44 CSS pixels.

## Source note (draft vs. Recommendation)

An earlier Candidate Recommendation draft (https://www.w3.org/TR/2023/CR-WCAG22-20230124/) words the 2.5.8 spacing exception differently — 'The target does not overlap any other target and has a target offset of at least 24 CSS pixels to every adjacent target' — and omits the 'legally required' clause in the Essential exception. That wording is superseded. Against the **published Recommendation**, the correct formulation is the **24 CSS pixel diameter circle centered on each target's bounding box**, which is what is reported above. If you are auditing against a document that still cites the CR text, cite the Recommendation instead.

## Reference summary for reuse

- SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) — Level AA — minimum 24 × 24 CSS px — spacing exception: 24 CSS px diameter circle, no intersection.
- SC 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced) — Level AAA — minimum 44 × 44 CSS px — no spacing exception.
- CSS px values are WCAG reference pixels, independent of device pixel density.

question: X18
answer:
# AES-GCM parameter limits under NIST SP 800-38D (November 2007), RBG-based IV construction

## 1. Answers at a glance

| # | Question | Answer | Clause |
|---|----------|--------|--------|
| 1 | IV length implementations should restrict support to | **96 bits (12 bytes)** | §5.2.1.1 (recommendation); §8.2.2 (r ≥ 96 for RBG-based IVs) |
| 2 | Max total invocations of the authenticated encryption function under one key | **2^32 = 4,294,967,296** | §8.3 |
| 3 | Max plaintext length per invocation | **2^39 − 256 bits = 2^36 − 32 = 68,719,476,704 bytes** | §5.2.1.1 |

All three are properties of the standard, not of any particular implementation. The RBG-based construction is assumed throughout (§8.2.2), which is the construction that triggers the §8.3 invocation cap.

---

## 2. Ask 1 — IV length: 96 bits

**Basis.** §5.2.1.1 recommends that implementations restrict support to the IV length of 96 bits, to promote interoperability, efficiency, and simplicity of design.

**Why 96 bits is the right restriction under the RBG-based construction:**

1. **Direct J0, no GHASH.** At exactly 96 bits the IV is used verbatim as the pre-counter block, J0 = IV || 0^31 || 1. For any other supported length, J0 = GHASH_H(IV || 0^s || [len(IV)]_64), which introduces a second collision surface (repeated J0 for distinct IVs) on top of IV repetition itself. Fixing 96 bits removes that surface entirely.
2. **Minimum admissible RBG length.** Under §8.2.2 the RBG-based construction's random field must satisfy r ≥ 96 bits, and for a given IV length r is fixed for the life of the key. At 96 bits the whole IV is random field, the free field is empty, and every IV bit carries randomness — the most efficient use of the RBG output.
3. **Keeps the birthday analysis tight.** With a single fixed IV length per key and q = 2^32 invocations, the IV-repeat probability is C(q,2)/2^96 ≈ 2^63/2^96 = 2^-33, which satisfies the 2^-32 upper bound mandated at the head of §8. Mixing multiple IV lengths under one key complicates this accounting without improving security.

**If other lengths must be supported anyway**, §8.2.2 constrains the choice, and these constraints must be enforced across *all* instances using the key:

- For any supported IV length strictly less than 96 bits, the RBG-based construction (§8.2.2) *shall* be used.
- For any supported IV length of 96 bits or greater, exactly one of the two constructions — not both — shall be used, consistently.
- The IV length (and r) must be fixed for the life of the key per length.

Supporting 96 bits only is therefore the recommended and simplest compliant configuration; it does **not** by itself exempt you from the invocation cap in Ask 2 (see below).

---

## 3. Ask 2 — Maximum invocations per key: 2^32 = 4,294,967,296

**Basis — §8.3, "Constraints on the Number of Invocations":**

> The total number of invocations of the authenticated encryption function shall not exceed 2^32, including all IV lengths and all instances of the authenticated encryption function with the given key.

**Scope of the requirement.** §8.3 applies to all implementations that use either (1) the deterministic construction with IVs whose length is not 96 bits, or (2) the RBG-based construction for IVs of any length. Equivalently: *unless an implementation only uses 96-bit IVs generated by the deterministic construction*, the 2^32 cap applies.

Because this question specifies **RBG-based IVs**, the cap applies at full force regardless of IV length — including the 96-bit case. Do not read the Ask 1 answer as an exemption; the 96-bit exemption in §8.3 is available only to the *deterministic* construction.

**Interpretation details that matter for implementation:**

- The count is **global per key**, not per instance: it aggregates every device, thread, process, and IV length using that key. The standard explicitly calls this a global requirement to be achieved by appropriate local limits per instance; its worked example limits each of 2^10 devices to 2^20 invocations at 64-bit IVs, 2^21 at 96-bit IVs, and 2^20 at 128-bit IVs.
- It counts invocations of the **authenticated encryption** function only. Authenticated *decryption* invocations are governed separately (Appendix C tables), not by §8.3.
- The bound is justified by the birthday/collision argument: with q = 2^32 IVs, the probability of a repeated IV is ≈ q^2/2^(r+1); for r = 96 this is ≈ 2^-33, just inside the 2^-32 ceiling. q = 2^32.5 would breach it, so 2^32 is not arbitrary slack.
- Consequence: a key may not be used indefinitely. Operationally, provision key rotation (or per-context key derivation) so that no key ever approaches 2^32 encryptions, and treat the counter as a hard, checked resource rather than an advisory statistic.

**Enforcement sketch (application layer):**

```text
state per key:  invocations_used : uint64   # durable, shared across all instances
                iv_length_bits  : fixed at key provision time (96)

seal(key, plaintext, aad):
    if invocations_used >= 2^32:                 # 4294967296
        raise KeyExhaustedError(key_id)          # fail closed; emit no ciphertext
    if len(plaintext) > 68719476704:             # 2^36 - 32 bytes, Ask 3
        raise PlaintextTooLongError(len(plaintext))
    iv = RBG(96 bits)                            # §8.2.2, fresh per invocation
    (C, T) = GCM_Encrypt(key, iv, plaintext, aad)
    invocations_used += 1                        # persist atomically before returning C
    return (iv, C, T)
```

The counter increment must be committed atomically (or the reservation made durably) *before* the ciphertext leaves the process; otherwise a crash-restart loop can silently overshoot 2^32. In a distributed deployment with per-node keys, each node holds its own counter but the sum over nodes sharing a key must still stay ≤ 2^32 — the cleanest guarantee is to give each node a distinct key (or derive per-node keys) and budget each one below the cap.

---

## 4. Ask 3 — Maximum plaintext per invocation: 68,719,476,704 bytes

**Basis — §5.2.1.1:** the bit length of the plaintext, len(P), shall not exceed **2^39 − 256 bits**.

**Where the −256 comes from.** GCTR consumes the plaintext in 128-bit blocks driven by inc32 on the low 32 bits of the counter block. The 32-bit counter space covers 2^32 blocks = 2^39 bits of keystream, but the last block is reserved so the counter cannot wrap and reuse a block (which would reuse keystream and destroy confidentiality). Hence the plaintext maximum is 2^39 − 2^7 = 2^39 − 256 bits.

**Conversion to bytes (the unit the question asks for):**

```
(2^39 − 256) bits / 8 = 2^36 − 32 bytes
2^36                = 68,719,476,736
68,719,476,736 − 32 = 68,719,476,704 bytes
```

Equivalently 64 GiB − 32 bytes. Bit-level check: 2^39 = 549,755,813,888; minus 256 = 549,755,813,632 bits; ÷ 8 = 68,719,476,704 bytes. ✔

**Correction to a widely repeated error (including in this request's own assumption table).** The figure "2^39 − 256 bits, i.e. 2^32 − 2 octets = 4,294,967,294 bytes" is arithmetically wrong: 4,294,967,294 bytes = 2^35 − 16 bits, a factor of 16 below the actual limit. The correct byte value is **2^36 − 32 = 68,719,476,704 bytes**. Any implementation enforcing 4,294,967,294 bytes is enforcing a limit roughly 16× stricter than the standard requires (harmless for security but non-conforming for interoperability and needlessly restrictive for large-object encryption).

**What this bound does and does not cover:**

- It is a bound on **plaintext** only. The AAD has its own, much larger cap: len(A) ≤ 2^64 − 1 bits (§5.2.1.1). The two are separate constraints, not a shared budget.
- The authentication tag length t does not enter this bound. However, if short tags are in use (t = 32 or 64 bits), Appendix C imposes far smaller per-invocation limits on the combined ciphertext + AAD length; those override the 2^39 − 256 figure for those configurations. The 68,719,476,704-byte answer assumes a full-strength tag (t = 128, or at least t ≥ 96).
- This per-invocation bound and the 2^32 per-key invocation bound are independent: both must hold simultaneously. Their product (≈ 2^68 bytes of plaintext per key at both limits) is not itself a standard-defined limit — it is simply the envelope you get by taking both maxima at once, and it exceeds any practical storage volume, so in practice key lifetime will be driven by the invocation counter or by policy, not by data volume.

---

## 5. Consistency cross-check of the stated values

| Quantity | Value | Check |
|---|---|---|
| IV length | 96 bits | ≥ 96 (RBG random-field minimum, §8.2.2); whole IV is random field, free field empty |
| Invocations per key | 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 | IV-repeat prob. ≈ 2^63/2^96 = 2^-33 ≤ 2^-32 (§8 mandated ceiling) ✔ |
| Max plaintext | 2^39 − 256 bits | = 2^32 − 1 counter blocks used for data, last block reserved ✔ |
| Max plaintext in bytes | 2^36 − 32 = 68,719,476,704 | (2^39 − 256)/8 exactly ✔ |
| AAD max | 2^64 − 1 bits | Separate bound, not a shared budget with plaintext ✔ |

No stated value violates any threshold set elsewhere in this deliverable. The 2^32 invocation cap remains in force even after restricting to 96-bit IVs, because the IVs are RBG-generated, not deterministically generated.

---

## 6. Scope and assumptions

- **Edition.** NIST SP 800-38D, November 2007 (final). No revision, addendum, or draft revision (SP 800-38D Rev. 1 / wGCM work) is applied; those are not the authoritative text for these three questions and would change the numbers.
- **Construction.** RBG-based IV construction (§8.2.2), IV length fixed at 96 bits for the life of the key. The deterministic-construction exemption in §8.3 is therefore *not* available.
- **Cipher.** AES-128/192/256 — the three limits above are independent of key size; only the IV length, the per-key invocation count, and the per-invocation plaintext length matter.
- **Units.** Ask 1 is stated in bits (96, = 12 bytes); Ask 2 is a count of function invocations; Ask 3 is stated in bytes as requested (68,719,476,704 = 2^36 − 32), with its bit-level origin (2^39 − 256) given for traceability.

Scope: this answer applies to unmodified upstream PostgreSQL 18. Vendor builds or wrappers can patch or override initdb defaults, so verify the resulting cluster with the checks below.

1. Default state with no checksum-related option

Yes. In PostgreSQL 18, initdb defaults to enabling data checksums. The initdb documentation for -k/--data-checksums says: 'This is enabled by default; use --no-data-checksums to disable checksums.' The PostgreSQL 18.0 release notes say: 'Change initdb default to enable data checksums' and 'Checksums can be disabled with the new initdb option --no-data-checksums.' Therefore:

  initdb -D /var/lib/pgsql/18/data

creates a cluster with data checksums enabled. Passing -k/--data-checksums is redundant, though harmless. The pre-18 default was off, so this is a behavior change.

Verify the state:

  # Running cluster
  psql -Atc 'SHOW data_checksums;'
  # Expected: on

  # Stopped cluster, or immediately after initdb
  pg_controldata -D /var/lib/pgsql/18/data | grep 'Data page checksum version'
  # Expected: 1 = enabled, 0 = disabled

2. Switching data checksums off

There are two supported mechanisms.

A. At initialization, preferred for a new empty cluster:

  initdb -D /var/lib/pgsql/18/data --no-data-checksums

This is the new PostgreSQL 18 option. If the cluster was just created with the default and has no data, remove the empty data directory and re-run initdb with --no-data-checksums.

B. On an existing cluster, as an offline operation:

  pg_ctl -D /var/lib/pgsql/18/data stop -m fast
  pg_checksums --disable --progress -D /var/lib/pgsql/18/data
  pg_ctl -D /var/lib/pgsql/18/data start

pg_checksums must run with the server stopped and with exclusive access to the data directory. It operates at the full-cluster level; checksums cannot be enabled or disabled per database or per table. Take a backup first. The operation can take time on a large cluster.

What is not a switch-off:

  - data_checksums is a read-only configuration variable. SET data_checksums = off and ALTER SYSTEM SET data_checksums = off do not work.
  - ignore_checksum_failure only bypasses checksum verification when reading a page during recovery. It does not remove checksums or disable checksum calculation, and should be used only temporarily for corruption recovery.
  - There is no supported online toggle for data checksums.

3. pg_upgrade constraint and procedure

The old cluster and the new cluster must have the same data checksum setting: both enabled or both disabled. pg_upgrade does not convert checksums during the upgrade. The 18.0 release notes state: 'pg_upgrade requires matching cluster checksum settings, so this new option can be useful to upgrade non-checksum old clusters.' The pg_upgrade documentation says to initialize the new cluster with compatible initdb flags that match the old cluster, and that pg_upgrade checks pg_controldata for compatible settings before starting the upgrade.

Procedure:

  a. Determine the old cluster checksum state:

     # If the old cluster is running
     psql -Atc 'SHOW data_checksums;'

     # If the old cluster is stopped
     pg_controldata -D /old/data | grep 'Data page checksum version'

  b. Stop the old cluster cleanly before pg_upgrade.

  c. Initialize the new PostgreSQL 18 cluster with the matching state:

     # Old cluster has checksums enabled, version 1
     initdb -D /new/data
     # or explicitly: initdb -D /new/data --data-checksums

     # Old cluster has checksums disabled, version 0
     initdb -D /new/data --no-data-checksums

     Do not start the new cluster. pg_upgrade does not require it to be started.

  d. If the new cluster was already initialized with the wrong setting, either re-initialize it, which is simplest for an empty cluster, or while it is stopped run one of:

     pg_checksums --disable -D /new/data
     pg_checksums --enable  -D /new/data

     Use --disable to match an old cluster with checksums off, and --enable to match an old cluster with checksums on.

  e. Run pg_upgrade --check first, with your normal pg_upgrade arguments, for example:

     pg_upgrade --check -b /old/bin -B /new/bin -d /old/data -D /new/data

     A checksum mismatch is an incompatibility. Do not proceed if --check fails.

  f. Run the real pg_upgrade only after --check passes.

  g. Start the new cluster and verify that its checksum state matches the old cluster:

     psql -Atc 'SHOW data_checksums;'
     pg_controldata -D /new/data | grep 'Data page checksum version'

Important cases:

  - Old cluster is pre-18 and was created with no checksum option: the old cluster is off. The new PostgreSQL 18 default is on, so the new cluster must be initialized with --no-data-checksums, or checksums must be enabled on the old cluster offline before the upgrade if checksums are wanted afterward. The first path is the low-risk path described by the release note.
  - Old cluster is PostgreSQL 18 and was created with no checksum option: the old cluster is on, so the new cluster's default initdb behavior matches.
  - If checksum state is to be changed after the upgrade, do it as a separate offline pg_checksums operation after pg_upgrade, not during pg_upgrade.
  - pg_upgrade --link and --swap do not relax the checksum-match requirement. If --link is used, do not run pg_checksums on the old cluster after linking; make any checksum changes before pg_upgrade.
  - The checksum setting is stored in pg_control and reflected by the read-only data_checksums variable; editing postgresql.conf does not change it.

Verification matrix:

  Old pg_controldata 1 -> new initdb default or --data-checksums -> new pg_controldata 1 -> pg_upgrade --check passes
  Old pg_controldata 0 -> new initdb --no-data-checksums       -> new pg_controldata 0 -> pg_upgrade --check passes
  Old pg_controldata 1 -> new initdb --no-data-checksums       -> mismatch -> pg_upgrade --check fails
  Old pg_controldata 0 -> new initdb default                   -> mismatch -> pg_upgrade --check fails

supported(A, K) := (K <= A) AND ((A - K) <= limit(K))

limit(K) := 2   if K < 25      # the parenthetical exception
